War Appropriation
BRITISH	COLUMBIA-HUNGER STRIKES-PROCE-
On the orders of the day:

I should like to ask the Minister
of Labour two questions with respect to a matter which I believe is of urgent national importance, owing to the prominence it has received in the Vancouver Daily Province of April 27. What steps are being taken to maintain the prestige of the authorities in connection with the hunger strikes by the Japanese in British Columbia? Are wealthy Japanese allowed to settle wherever they see fit, and in whatever manner they desire, for the duration?

My reply to the first question is that any Japanese guilty of breach of discipline are being promptly dealt with by the British Columbia security commission, and those who do not comply with instructions are immediately interned. With regard to the second question, no Japanese, regardless of their financial standing, are being allowed to relocate in any part of British Columbia or anywhere else without first receiving the permission of the security commission.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: Thev house resumed from Tuesday, April 28, consideration in committee of a resolution to provide sums not exceeding $2,000,000,000 for the year ending March 31, 1943, for granting to his majesty aid for national defence and security-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
As a member of the
house I believe I have the right to speak on matters of vital importance, despite the fact that I happen to be a member of the armed forces. Naturally there are certain limitations with respect to what I can or should say, and I shall follow the procedure in the British House of Commons. Having due regard to those limitations I shall endeavour to bring before the house certain matters which I consider it is my duty to discuss. There are a number of things I may say here, and a number I may say in another place. I shall endeavour to keep the subjects I may discuss here separate .from those of another nature which may be discussed elsewhere.
Discussing Canada's war effort a British general, not now in Canada, said to me the
other day, "One of the greatest difficulties you have in Canada, one of the besetting sins of the Canadian war effort, is the office-bound staff."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The office-bound staff?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes, and by that he
meant that the officers on the various staffs do not visit the training establishments as they should do. I believe I have had a rather unique experience in that not only have I had the opportunity and the ability on frequent occasions to visit national defence headquarters, but I have been in the districts and with the field formations. What we are up against in the army to-day is the task of correlating our points of view. There is a certain point of view in national defence headquarters, a second point of view in the districts, and still another point of view in the field formations. All the difficulties which have arisen have been largely due to the fact that the points of view of the districts, the field formations and national defence headquarters have been divergent. We have tried to work as a unit by carrying on too much correspondence, and that is the first point I wish to discuss to-day.
In over two years of war I have had only one visit in my own branch from a superior officer attached to national defence headquarters. I suggest that visits between the districts and headquarters should be very frequent, and I also suggest that the district staff officers should have more opportunity to visit the field formations. To show the enormous size of the work may I point out that during the last year I travelled between 25,000 and 30,000 miles for the department. Even so, there were in one district two establishments I was not able to visit in that one year. That is the first problem we are up against.
I would suggest that the training officers should be rotated between the basic and advanced training centres and by headquarters. The officers responsible for the training of the Canadian army would then have the point of view not only of headquarters but of the districts and the training centres themselves. We have tried to do this by correspondence, but the main difficulty is the fact that correspondence ties officers to their desks at headquarters. One visit of a training officer, even a junior officer, to the training centres would do more good than all the correspondence one could write. I believe they should be rotated.
I wonder whether the house realizes the complexity of the Canadian army to-day. First you have the headquarters establish-
War Appropriation

meat, then the districts, then the command headquarters, then the basic training centres, advanced training centres, technical training schools, veterans' guards companies, specialized units, and active army units in the fourth division. Each of these units has a definite and unique part to play. Unless the members of these units are rotated with their own headquarters, we shall not achieve the true efficiency that we should have in our army.
I should like to mention one or two matters as examples. I would refer first to the syllabus for physical training. The training centre officers tell me that with the PT syllabus now in effect they find it difficult to keep the interest of the men. They have no authority to alter this basic training syllabus. Our training is in a constant state of evolution, and they tell me that if this syllabus were modified even slightly it would help the morale of the troops and make them more keen about their training. Hon. members will realize that it would be manifestly impossible to allow the officers at the training centres to alter the training syllabus as they wished. But I do suggest that there should be an opportunity for the officers in the directorate of military training at Ottawa to go to these basic training centres and find out how these syllabuses could be altered. Our training changes after practically every new action or campaign fought in the war.
Another matter has to do with the basic training centres. The first thing you try to do with a new recruit is to make him enthusiastic about the army. The first few days in the army constitute a most vital part of the young man's military life. The first thing you do is to give the young man an old Ross rifle, dated 1905, probably with the bolt missing or the sight gone. He is told that this is to be his personal weapon of protection. This rifle may be all right for drill purposes, but it is good for nothing else and the psychological reaction is bad. I believe the department should consider providing a complete set of the most modern weapons for each basic training centre so that the young soldier, instead of seeing these dreadful old guns, can be shown the modern Lee-Enfield rifle, the two-inch or three-inch mortars and the rest of the excellent weapons we have. I understand that in the United States army the first thing they do with their recruit is to take him out on the range, give him a rifle, and tell him that there is the target, try to hit it. He is thus given confidence in his weapon. I mention these old Ross rifles as a sample of what we are up against.
Then there is the selection of men for the specialized branches. This selection is made

at the basic training centres which I consider a most important part of our army. The raw recruit comes into the basic training centre, in most cases wanting to do a job. After h$ has spent the prescribed time there, he is selected to go into the infantry, the artillery, the ordnance, the signals, the medical corps or some other branch of the army. This is just one more reason why we should do everything in our power to provide adequate equipment. With such equipment we would be able to find out more about the capabilities of our troops.
The next step is from the basic to the advanced training centre. In the advanced training centre considerably more equipment is available. Naturally you cannot teach a man to run before he walks, and a much better job of equipping is done at the advanced training centres. It is here that the soldier really begins to appreciate his responsibilities. It is here that he realizes the job ahead of him. He begins to realize what a lot he has to learn. Here again I earnestly suggest that training officers be rotated so that the advanced training officer in the advanced training centre will know the difficulties which the district headquarters are up against and what national defence headquarters is up against. If the officers were rotated in this way, a tremendous amount of correspondence that is now carried on would be eliminated.
From the point of view again of the advanced training officer, he is trying to do a job; he is up against a difficulty; he is out with the troops. He explains that difficulty in writing as well as he can, and it has to go through the district headquarters and from there to national defence headquarters. If the officer at national defence headquarters would come to the training centre and spend a day in the field; if he would perhaps live for a month at the advanced training centre, the advanced training officer could explain to him in ten minutes what he is up against, rather than have to put it in writing and send it through the usual channels. In this war of movement time is absolutely vital, and time is just as vital in training as it is in actual combat. I do suggest that this method would speed up your training and make it more efficient.
Stonewall Jackson said this about war:
War means fighting. The business of the soldier is to fight. Armies are not called out to dig trenches, to throw up breastworks, to live in camps, but to find the enemy and strike him; to invade his country and do him all possible damage in the shortest possible time. This will involve great destruction of life and property while it lasts; but such a war will be of necessity of brief continuance, and so would be an economy of life and property, in

War Appropriation
the end. To move swiftly, strike vigorously, and secure all the fruits of victory is the secret of successful war.
If anything has shown that he was right when he said that, it has been the successful campaigns of the German army in the present war. Each of them has been violent, rapid, and tremendously destructive, but I think it can also be said of them that they were all economical of life compared with a long campaign of attrition, compared with battles like Passchendaele in the last war, compared with trench warfare. If we are to defeat the powers arrayed against us, the type of warfare described by Stonewall Jackson is the type of warfare we shall have to fight. I believe that is generally realized, but it must be driven home every day to every officer and every soldier in the Canadian army that tremendous speed is essential.
Officers returning from the recent campaign in Libya-we have seen quite a number of them and have talked with them-have said that one of their difficulties was the breakdown of communications, the lack of coordination, shall I say, between the air force and the army. In this war every man, particularly every officer, and more particularly every staff officer, has to think in a three-dimensional plane. If you are in the army you must think also of the air force. If you are in the air force you must think also of the army. You must know the limitations of the weapons of the sister forces, their capabilities and their characteristics. I suggest to the government that that is one of the things we in Canada are not teaching. I suggest that there should be a joint staff of officers who are trained in the air and on the ground. I make that suggestion most sincerely. Suppose an air officer is put in a tank. At once he gets an entirely new conception of its limitations of vision, the hazards of ground, and other features of tank warfare. Or put a tank officer from one of the armoured divisions in the air, and at once he gets an entirely new conception of camouflaging his tank, of its vulnerability, its ability to move with speed and a thousand and one other things. It is an extremely technical matter and one that requires constant study. One requisite in the army to-day is constant education. No one should be in the army who is not prepared to work at his job and to learn all the time. Every new campaign has new lessons to teach. Let me give an example of the sort of thing that happens at the present time.
The other day in England an officer wanted photographs taken of a certain area. He telephoned to the local air force command saying he wanted those photographs taken. The air
force commander asked, "What is your ceiling there?" The army officer could not tell him what his ceiling was. He did not know as elementary a thing as that about the sister force. Every army officer who is in charge of the movement of troops should be able to cooperate with the air force and know and understand the limitations of aircraft. Here, simply because of a lack of knowledge of the air arm, a request was made which it was impossible to carry out.
There are one or two small points I might also mention. There have been a number of accidents to mechanical transport. We have standing accident boards. They have them in England. The air force asked me, "What are you people doing about night blindness?"
I do not know what is being done about night blindness, but we have had quite a number of accidents which have been caused by people whose vision at night was faulty, who were suffering from some degree of night blindness. Here is another example of how the air force and the army can cooperate. I do not know what is being done about night blindness, but the subject is very important. To a man driving extremely valuable equipment, and going into action in the dark, vision is one of the most essential things. We have found that many accidents in England have been caused by night blindness.
A word about discipline. It is no secret that one of the principal troubles is absence without leave. It is not as general as many people think, but it does exist, and is probably responsible for 80 per cent of detention crime in this country. Absence without leave is punishable by stopping a man's pay, perhaps for fourteen, perhaps for twenty-eight days, but the loss of pay goes on much longer than that because his allowance is paid to his wife and family, while he draws no pay on pay day. His psychological reaction is a loss of interest in the army; his attitude is, "what's the use?" This matter has been brought to my notice, as a member of this house, by constituents of mine who are in the army. They say, "We lose heart when we find that we are not to get any pay for a month, or even two months. There is no incentive to do well; why should we not go absent without leave again?" One tries to argue with such a man, but his is really a psychopathic case; a great deal of work has to be done on it, and if the condition goes on for a considerable time, his wife, family and dependents suffer also. I have a suggestion to make in that connection in a minute.
Another point I want to mention is that a great many soldiers have to wait a considerable time for district courts-martial. The judge
War Appropriation

advocate-general's department is required to prepare cases for courts-martial, and nearly all of them are for absence without leave. They are always very busy.
My suggestion is that the training centre commandants be given more power to deal summarily with these cases. There should be some system of immediate punishment, such as punishment drill, so that the man who is on leave and is tempted to outstay it will reflect, "I shall have to walk up that so-and-so hill a dozen times if I don't get back to the camp in time", and will make every effort to avoid the penalty. Let the punishment be immediate. Do not keep men hanging around in detention, not carrying on training, waiting for district courts-martial. Remember that we are terribly short of time for training.
There are a few other matters, concerning dependents' allowances, which I think should be brought before the committee. First let me mention the matter of soldiers' children. The soldier, going overseas, leaves his wife and family here in Canada. The wife gets a job in a munitions factory, and there is, I think, every reason why she should. It is important that everybody should be usefully employed, and many of these women are doing an excellent job. But they leave for work at an early hour in the morning and they do not get back before six o'clock at night. In the interval the children are entirely without parental supervision. Consequently we find in Toronto -and I believe the situation is general-a large increase of delinquency among children. I suggest that the minister's department should consult with other departments to see whether something cannot be done such as they are doing in England. In the schools of England a meal is provided at mid-day for the child whose parents are working. Also they have established certain types of nursery schools to take care of the children of soldiers and others whose work prevents them from remaining at home. Nothing can be more upsetting to the soldier overseas than to read in the newspaper or have somebody report to him that his eight-year-old boy has been haled before the children's court for stealing chocolate bars or throwing stones through a window. This is a matter for interdepartmental cooperation, and it should be attended to right away, for it affects the morale of the army. The soldier concludes that we who are still in Canada are not looking after his dependents, and there is nothing more likely to destroy his confidence in the cause for which he is fighting.
I have had mothers come to me and say, 'T get no allowance although my boy is in the army, because he was on relief before he
fMr. Adamson.]
joined up and was not contributing to my support." For that reason, it appears, the department take the attitude that they should not be held responsible for the support of the mother. That attitude, it seems to me, is definitely wrong and false. It penalizes the soldier. If the man does not go into the army he can get work at $6 or $7 a day and thus support his mother, but if he enlists she is penalized because he was previously unemployed. Some attention should be paid to that, and very quickly.

No. I started long before that.
Another matter that I have in mind has reference to pensions in respect of men killed or injured in Canada. Very often men have been on leave, on pass away from military duty, and have been injured or killed, but the department has taken the attitude that it was no responsibility of theirs. That attitude should be reviewed. I consider it is the responsibility of the government just as much in Canada as in England.
I leave these suggestions with the government. The most important thing of all is to see to it, from the point of view of headquarters, from the point of view of field formation, that there is correlation. Do not do it by letter. Let us have an interchange of views so that we can get down to brass tacks with the men actually in the camps and training centres so that we shall know

War Appropriation
what we are trying to do, and so that they will know our difficulties and we shall know theirs. Five minutes spent in such discussion is worth all the correspondence in the world.
I am not going to bring up the question of reserves, nor am I going to bring up the question of home defence personnel in the active army, except to say this. I believe that the Canadian army should be the Canadian army and that, now that the plebiscite is over, there should be no distinction as to where a man serves. The sooner we can do away with home defence personnel in active units, the better it will be because we shall then be able to strike the greatest blow for improved morale in the Canadian army.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend has mentioned quite a number of points that may be interesting to other members of the committee and perhaps I might be permitted to deal with them, though not at length, to indicate to hon. members what has been done and what is being done along the lines to which the hon. gentleman has referred. I do not think he does the British officer whom he quotes quite justice. I am not quite satisfied that the British officer, if he is of the type of British officer I know, made any such statement as that the besetting sin of the Canadian war effort was the office-bound staff. I know British officers well enough to know that they do not criticize in that tone or spirit, and I suggest to my hon. friend that he make the criticism his own and not bolster it up with a statement by a British officer whose name he does not give and whom, I am satisfied, he misquotes in using that expression.
My hon. friend has referred to the matter of personal contact between headquarters and districts. He has referred to something that is so elementary that I do not think it needs much emphasis from any of us. We all understand that if it were possible by personal visit to indicate all the things that have to be communicated in connection with the army or in connection with business, it would be highly desirable to do so, supplementing it with matters on record, so that people will not misunderstand what has been said. That is impossible in connection with the army and has been from the beginning. We have been just as busy as we could be in raising, equipping, organizing, feeding, clothing and transporting the army, but there has been no possibility of building up this staff as we should have liked to build it up. I know there is some criticism in this house in certain quarters, indicating that we have too much staff. I say to you, Mr. Chairman,
that this view is not shared by very many who know the organization of the armed forces, either navy, army or air.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: You do not say anything about the source of the criticism.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
What I am endeavouring to do, and I say this frankly, is to increase the staff in order to meet the very natural demand which comes from all quarters, not simply from districts but from headquarters as well, for particulars, to study problems on the ground, to meet with officers on the firing line, if I may put it that way, and to endeavour to assist in their problems. My hon. friend is aware, I know, that I do not profess to suggest for a moment that the liaison has been perfect, but I do suggest that there has been considerable; and the fact that he as an intelligence officer has not been officially called to headquarters, or that he has had only one visit from an intelligence officer at headquarters, does not by any means represent the liaison between headquarters and officers in the district.
Let me say this in connection with the district officers commanding. As my hon. friend knows, there was, as soon as the chief of the general staff and I came back from England a year ago, an immediate conference of D.O.C.'s from all over the dominion. We cannot have them in very often, but we brought them in then to discuss the whole matter with regard to the war prospects, and they were brought in again only quite recently. But that does not represent liaison, because, particularly in some parts of the country which have been concerned with regard to their defence, there have been visits from senior officers from headquarters. I instance the chief of the general staff who in December, went to the Pacific coast, and the vicechief of the general staff, who went at the time I went to the Pacific coast, or three months thereafter. The chief of the general staff has been on both coasts, and so far as the staff officers are concerned, I have made it a rule in connection with every convoy to see that some senior staff officer is there.
Perhaps I might give to the committee a list of the conferences which have been held at headquarters. That means officers coming from districts. The D.O.C. conference was held some time ago, and there was another in March this year. The A.A.Q.M.G.'s held a conference, and district recruiting officers held two conferences in the last six months-about six months. In January we had a conference of commandants of all basic training centres straight across Canada, and this is a matter
War Appropriation

to which my hon. friend devoted a considerable portion of his remarks, namely, work in the basic training centres. We brought the commandants of the basic training centres in in the month of January, and we had a conference of commandants and officers of training centres and advanced training centres as well. That was the middle of last year, the latter half of the year. We had a general staff officers conference in September and district ordnance officers conferences in October, 1941, and February, 1942. At the present time the chief of the general staff, with Brigadier Weeks, who is officer in charge of training, and a deputy chief of the general staff, and Brigadier Macklin, from the adjutant-general's branch, are on a ten-days' tour. They are not attempting to cover all Canada by any means but are making a meticulous visit to all training centres in Ontario. They will be out for something like ten days. As a matter of fact we have arranged the organization of the general staff so that we shall have an officer on the road practically all the time in connection with training. We have so arranged it that there are two officers under Brigadier Weeks, that is, Colonel Whitelaw, who is in charge of the regular military training, and under him is Colonel Sparling, who was overseas and who now has come back. In the other branch of training we have Colonel Kennedy, who is director of trades training and who also came back from overseas for the purpose of taking up that work. Then we have a liaison officer who himself can go out, or who can take the position of officers in the department in order to permit them to go out.
In connection with this matter of training my hon. friend lays down again what I think are some pretty elementary principles. He says that at the basic training centres-I believe this was the expression he used-there should be a full or complete set of the most modern weapons, and he deprecated very much the idea of issuing what he called the old Ross rifle. I wish to assure my hon. friend that there are not very many new Ross rifles in the Dominion of Canada or anywhere else. There are not very many new mark I Lees, or new mark II Lees, or new mark III Lees. These are old rifles, but that does not interfere with their efficiency. I suggest to the committee that while we would like to supply all basic training centres with complete sets of the most modern weapons, we in this country have some obligation to the people who are on the firing lines at the present moment, who are using weapons of that kind and who are calling for more. Speaking for myself, I do not propose to take the position that we will insist on having the most modern

weapons in the basic training centres in Canada when they are needed more urgently elsewhere, where the fighting is active.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am not denying it at all. I am saying that rifles issued at the basic training centres are, generally speaking, not Ross rifles with the bolts out. I want to tell my hon. friend that these rifles are issued for the purpose of teaching musketry, and the recruits are given sufficient rifles with which

War Appropriation
to fire. I say to the committee quite frankly that I propose to follow this course until we have enough rifles for active work. I find that there has been practically no complaint from the basic training centres in that connection.
Let us understand this rifle situation. I have indicated before, and I have never concealed from the house, that the rifle situation is not as we would like to have it. At the same time we are doing everything we can to use the rifles we have to the best advantage, in the places where they are most needed, having regard to their condition. If my hon. friend and the committee knew as much as I do with regard to requirements for rifles in connection with this war, there would not be any complaint as to the fact that Ross rifles, some of them even without bolts, happen to be used in the basic training centres. We cannot issue complete sets of the most modern weapons to the basic training centres. Further, the training carried on there is not being carried on by those of us who have not been overseas in this war. It is being carried on by men who have come back from England and who know what training is going on there for the sort of warfare that we anticipate in this war.
I just want to give the committee a list in this connection. I have mentioned it before, but now I have the list under my hand. We have fourteen British officers here for three months as instructors. We have eleven officers from Canada on exchange with the British army at the present time. Some 93 officers have just returned to assume duties as second in command and as commanders of companies. Some 145 officers and 368 other ranks are now abroad or in transit for courses, and they will be brought back here later. Some 263 officers and 900 other ranks have just returned for instructional duties at advanced and basic training centres. That is the thousand men I mentioned the other night.

Thank you very much. Then seventy-two officers and other ranks have just returned from overseas after attachment for three months to the Canadian army overseas, and seventy-six are now going the other way for three months. These are the sort of men who are carrying on the training in these basic training centres. I do not profess to know very much about training. I can only give the syllabus as I have it, but
I want to say to the committee that the syllabus is under constant review by the training officers, who I think know their jobs fairly well. The changes are issued from month to month, as the opportunity arises. I would think-and I want to make sure about this, because my hon. friend struck a point in which I am very much interested- that the suggestion of a practical officer training men would receive the utmost attention and would be acted upon, unless there was something wrong with it. What my hon. friend said was that an officer at a training centre was not allowed to change the syllabus. Obviously you cannot have a syllabus prepared by people who we think understand what is required in that connection, and having due regard to the practice in the United Kingdom, and then have it changed at will by someone who thinks he knows a better way. But you can immediately take up any suggestion which is made by any officer. I agree with my hon. friend in this respect-and I have tried to preach it in connection with the Canadian army-that I believe not only is there always a difficulty in bringing together the people in the district and the people at headquarters, but there is a difficulty to some extent in bringing together the ranks themselves, that is to say the man who is very much senior and the man who is junior. The man who is junior is working away at his job, and he gets the idea that was expressed by my hon. friend, that any suggestion he makes will, of course, not be listened to by the people up top. As a result he does not make the suggestion. I have said I felt that our army, in order to get along and make the most of its opportunities, should have people pressing from the bottom up and from the top down in order to get together in connection with these matters.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is that known among the junior officers?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have tried to make it known, and I know the chief of the general staff has tried to make it known.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is just what I want to bring about, the interchange of junior officers. Do not send a general round to the basic training centres and try to get ideas from your junior officers. They will not give them to him.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Junior officers do not generally talk to the inspecting officer. The junior officer talks, I think, to the man with whom he works in the training centre. But the general, whoever he may be, is the man who has authority on the ground to make the change. I think that is the advantage of
War Appropriation

the minister going around once in a while. I say that because there are certain things which can be done off the bat. Otherwise, if you sent a junior officer he would have to write or to wire to his headquarters and be supported with documents. The result would be that the matter would get into the mails and it would be some time before action could be taken.
If at all possible, there is advantage in sending a senior officer who has power immediately to make a change or to give instructions that changes be made. There is no difficulty if the principle I suggest is adopted on the part of the senior as well as the junior officer, namely, that the senior officer sees to it that the junior officer's ideas are given a fair trial and a fair chance, and that they are receptive to suggestions which come in, notwithstanding the fact that they do not come from people on his staff.
The vice-chief of the general staff and I were out west for some time. I hope the committee will pardon my mentioning myself so much, but I make these observations simply to illustrate how time and again we ran across suggestions which had been made by a junior officer. We might find some equipment which was not there, and which the district did not know about. We would be told, "I have indented for it"-that is the favourite expression, as my hon. friend will know. That is the favourite word used in the district, the training centre or anywhere else.
. Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury): It means a requisition?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes, a requisition. It would mean that he has signed a request. Then he might get the idea that that is all that ought to be done. He may be discouraged and think that there is no use doing anything else, and that that is the army way of doing things. In the army you can get after a thing, indent, call up somebody on the telephone and say, "Did you get it; is it on your desk?" He probably finds it on his desk, with twenty or thirty other files. There may be need to deal with that quickly, but if it is not called particularly to a person's attention it may go to the bottom of a file, and . not be dealt with "for the next day or so. Then it may go next day to the master-general of the ordnance and be sorted' out there, with the result that it may take four or five days, or a week to deal with the matter. But in connection with a particular item a junior officer can follow it through. He can be encouraged to follow it through, either by telephone or otherwise; and if he were we would get certain things done that are necessary.

I beg the committee not to thirds that you can break down army or business routine and make it work. You will have chaos if you do. But you can have a sense of proportion in connection with the army, as well as with anything else. You can try to pick out things that are important.
Of course I am talking of departmental procedure. The danger is that a red tag may be placed on the file, marking it urgent. But everything of a routine nature will be tagged, with the result everything becomes urgent, and you are back to where you started. So I say there is room for initiative, and the actions of junior officers should be encouraged so that they would press, and do a little more than just indent. They should realize that their representations should not only receive consideration, but be acted upon.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

I do not know a great deal about the army, but I talk to officers who do know. Recently I had a conversation with an army officer with respect to this very matter of equipment. He made an observation to me which I shall pass on to the minister, because I believe it is sound. He said, "Is it not true that a man in training should, while training, have the weapons he proposes to use when he goes to war?" That is the idea, as briefly as I can express it. The minister has said it is not possible-and I quite agree. But should that not be the objective? It will be understood I am not raising this question with a view to reverting to the scolding the minister gave my colleague. I thought the minister was, perhaps, a little unfair, but I am content to let that pass. I suggest that the principle is sound, if it can be achieved. I believe it is a question of the ways and means, and the ability to achieve the objective.
The minister made it quite clear-and I agree with him-that if Lee-Enfield rifles are required elsewhere more than on our training fields, then they should be elsewhere. He will find no criticism I am sure from this side of the house on that score. But we are now in the war two and a half years, and I had thought that the rifle situation had improved. I should be glad if we were told just what the position is in that connection.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition has enunciated what I believe is an absolutely sound principle. I am not speaking as an expert, but it is obvious that if you can give a man the exact weapon he will use in the field, then that must be absolutely desirable. I agree that that should be the objective. I believe we have attained that at training centres with respect to every weapon except the rifle-and the hon. member for York

War Appropriation
West will have some information on that point. With respect to rifles we are using, shall I say, a different model from the rifle which may be used. As a matter of fact there are four marks of Lee-Enfields, two marks of Ross, besides the Springfields to which reference has been made. I could give the committee privately what the situation is in that regard; I believe I intimated it during the secret session. I can say only this, that the rifle situation is improving. It is improving very steadily, so far as production is concerned. The point is that demands, as well as production, are increasing; and that is the difficulty. The further point is that Canada's rifles are pretty well supposed to go round the world.
I referred to the officers who had been brought over from the other side, to indicate that there was liaison in that respect. I did not mention something which the hon. member for York West may know better than I, namely that conferences are held from time to time by the district officers commanding with the officers in command of units of the reserve army, and with the officers in command of the training centres in their districts; as well as of the active units in their districts.
I know that some general staff officers in charge of training pay visits more often than others. But what we are doing at headquarters, and have been doing-and we are endeavouring to do the same in the districts-is to go over the staff so that these visits can be made. So I leave that particular subject with the same thought with which I began the discussion of it by saying that I am thoroughly in accord with the idea as it has been expressed concerning the desirability of personal visits in every possible instance.
The hon. member mentioned joint operation. I do not believe the committee realizes just how closely the three arms of the service work. I have tried to make that clear before. We do work at headquarters through interservice committees. We have joint service committees on magazines, hospitals, pay and allowances, chemical warfare and conservation. We have a joint chiefs-of-staff committee which meets each week. We have a defence council which meets every week and which consists of the three ministers, three deputy ministers and the three chiefs of staff. There is the junior war staff at Kingston teaching combined operations. So really we are not neglectful of the principle which has been suggested, namely that as far as possible we should be familiar with the aims and work of the other armed services.
I am not in a position to give the committee further information with regard to the advance and progress which has been made along that line. But I can repeat what I said the other night, that definite progress is being made in connection with having the air force and the army combine and work together; and there are certain plans and programmes under way in Canada along the same line.
My hon. friend referred to night blindness. A great deal of research work is being done along that line. We have ordered machines for testing night blindness, and the testing will start just as soon as the machines are available. As a matter of fact there are more on order for the army. The hon. member mentioned absence without leave and suggested that the officer commanding be given more power.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, power to deal summarily with these cases.

I think I km right when I say that the officer commanding can give up to twenty-eight days' detention, and I should think that that is about power enough for the commanding officer. I believe the soldier has the right to elect to take court-martial if he so desires. I do not think we could give very much more. I would prefer not to give more power to the commanding officer than he has already, that is, the power to give twenty-eight days' detention, which in fact may mean twenty-eight days' imprisonment. As a matter of fact, that is the provision in' the army act. It does not follow that it is right simply because it is in the act or has been in force for many years, but one would think the test of time would have indicated that that is the extent of the power which should be given.
My hon. friend referred incidentally to the matter of creches for children of soldiers' wives. That is not strictly an army matter, but it has to do with the man-power problem. The problem to be considered by this country has to do with the drafting of women into industry in order to relieve men and make them available for the armed forces. I intended saying, when I was speaking just for a minute or two on that subject, that that was one of the many measures which has to be worked out and adopted if this plan of using women in industry is going to be effective. There are going to be married women who are soldiers' wives and married women who are not but who have children, and these children will have to be looked after if the services of the women are to be used in industry. It is not only a matter of training the women, it is not only a matter
War Appropriation

of moving them to industry, it is not only getting the employer to agree to have them; there is the additional problem of looking after their families while they are working.

speechtext: That was the important part of the question I was asking.

I just want to say a word or two about headquarters organization, in reply to the point raised by my hon. friend and along the line of what I have said already. My hon. friend suggested that the people at headquarters should go out more. There are two directorates of military training, one headed by Colonel Kennedy and the other by Colonel Whitelaw. In addition-I think I said this before-there is a liaison officer whose duty it is to travel to the training centres or to replace other section heads by staying at headquarters when they are travelling. I would say that the same principle is being developed in connection not only with the general staff but also with the adjutant-general's branch, the quartermaster-general's branch and the branch of the master-general of the ordnance. At this minute we have the quartermaster-general on the east coast, the master-general on the west coast heading east and the chief of the general staff with his deputy in charge of military training and one of the deputy adjutants-general travelling in central Canada. I am sure my hon. friend will not complain about the number of visitors from headquarters who are out on the road endeavouring to deal with the very problem to which he has referred.
I was dealing with the point raised by my hon. friend about junior officers not being able to amend the syllabus when I am afraid I got off on a pet hobby of mine. I am greatly interested in the necessity of paying attention to the recommendations of junior officers and seeing to it that we get the benefit of their views and experience. I only want to say that we are encouraging these suggestions. We are trying to get them through the officers in command of the basic training and advanced training centres. We are seeing to it that they do not fall by the wayside by providing these additional visitations from headquarters, either the district or national defence headquarters, in order to see that the suggestions are put into practice. As I say, we issue every month an amendment to the training syllabus embodying suggestions that we get from overseas and practices which we find from experience can be well adopted for our purposes. This is done in an endeavour to keep that training syllabus right up to date.

speechtext:
Because the comments I have made from time to time to the minister in connection with the administration of the

War Appropriation
army have not always been complimentary,
I should like to express my appreciation to the minister for his remarks to the house the other day and again to-day in defence of those who are administering the Canadian active army, particularly against the attacks of those whose military knowledge is, generally speaking, acquired from observing the army from a sidewalk. There have been times when I have expressed views in this house and in certain other places which were not complimentary to the individuals charged with the administration of the army, but generally speaking I believe that a bad dentist is better than a barber for a toothache, and an imperfect staff officer is probably more valuable to the administration of the army than many of those who criticize it. But having said that, may I add that I do not think there is any reason for the minister to be over-satisfied with the administration, nor do I think that he is absolutely satisfied.
Leaving the administration out of it for a moment or two, I should like to make some observations with respect to something new in the administration of the present army and offer some suggestions in connection therewith. I refer to the new basic training centre which has just been established and which has been designed to take care of those men who have been unable under the present set-up to assimilate the basic training during the period of two months which is assigned to them. I think everyone who has had anything to do with the administration and training of the present army will realize the need for such a training centre until those who are in the army have been helped to the point where they are able to take training in the basic or advanced training centres or are eliminated from the army. But, by the same token I would not like to see any development of that practice because I think it would be tackling the problem, which I suggest is a serious one, from the wrong end. It is true that we have a considerable number of men in the active army in Canada who either should not be there at all or require special consideration in order to enable them to keep up with those who are training. It is my hope, and certainly it is the policy of the department, that the personnel selection boards will be able to take care of that situation. I think perhaps in most districts at the present time they are doing a fair job in weeding out men who have been enlisted as physically perfect but who by reason of one handicap or another have been unable to keep up with the training in the basic training centres. In some cases they have got to the advanced training centres.
But that is tackling the problem after the men are in the army. I would like to have the assurance of the minister that something will be done to eliminate the necessity of such an institution as has been opened recently. The method of doing this does not matter a great deal so long as it is done, but I suggest that a personnel selection board officer might be attached to the various recruiting centres throughout the dominion to report on the recruits before attestation. I believe in that way you could eliminate within a comparatively short time the necessity of dealing with these men afterwards-these problem children, if you like to call them that, who are being provided for in the new basic training depot.
Arguments have been advanced against giving these men their examinations before they are attested. I know some of the difficulties in that connection because I am handling recruits every day that I am not here and have been doing so for nearly two years. At the same time, whatever the immediate cost and whatever the scarcity of suitable personnel selection board officers may be-and that is a real problem-I do not think this trouble should be allowed to grow.
About a year and a half ago some of us in this house were concerned over the fact that too many men, after having been duly enlisted and attested, were being discharged from the army before six months' training on the ground that they were not likely to make efficient soldiers. I expressed my opinion on that at that time; the regulations were tightened up, and the problem disappeared for some time. I suggest that it is in danger of recurring as a result of the weeding-out process which is now being carried on. Probably it is a good thing to insist on selection and intelligence tests for these men, certainly so long as we are able to get as many men as we can take care of in our present organization; nevertheless I believe the policy has been carried to an extreme. There have been cases and there are cases where adequately trained officers and men have been weeded out of their units at the age of thirty-three or thirty-four or thirty-five on the ground that they are too old. It seems to me that our Canadian army is thinking in terms of two and a half years of training, rather than in terms of what is the usual active life of a soldier, which is one hour or two. The worth of a soldier is determined by his courage and efficiency in action. There are all kinds of men who have been rejected for service who would live their hour, which is the life of a soldier, with gallantry and distinction but who have no place in the army at all, chiefly by reason of the fact that we have had
War Appropriation

very few casualties. We have been engaged in a two and a half years' endurance contest and great numbers of these men have not been able to make the grade. But that is not all it takes to make a soldier. I wonder if there are not here old soldiers of the last war who can remember the time when a forty or forty-five year old sergeant has had to carry on his back, figuratively speaking, some twenty or twenty-five year old subaltern until he found his feet. I wonder if there is anybody who was in the last war who does not remember the man we used to call the perfect soldier. Every company had one, almost every platoon, and in rank they ran all the way from corporal to colonel. They sat on a horse like a centaur, looked the part on parade, had a voice that could be heard for four blocks-in other words they had everything it took, except the courage to kill and die if necessary in the clutch, as the army calls it.
We have been concentrating on a perfect army. But even if we had a two-corps army composed entirely of men of the calibre of the commander I do not suppose it would, in the last analysis vitally affect the issue of this war. We are told that we have the best trained and most highly mechanized of all armies, but the experience of the last two and a half years has taught us that we must contemplate as a possibility our whole army, quite naturally and without any disgrace to themselves, entirely disappearing in the course of a forenoon. It seems to me that the department and the minister might give a little more attention to the expansion of the reserves of that army, and not so much attention to developing an overseas army of men who are super-soldiers. That is all right when you are preparing for a war five or six years from now, as we are told Hitler did, and we saw the effectiveness of that system at the beginning of the war.
There is one other thing I would draw to the attention of the minister. I understand at the present time it is not the policy of the department to allow any non-commissioned officer to proceed overseas with his rank. If I am correctly informed with respect to that-

speechtext: As a reinforcement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Quite so; then I would suggest to the minister that that is something which should be reconsidered. To begin with the difference between being a private and a sergeant in hundreds of instances is the difference, if you are a family man, between being able to enter the service and make anything like adequate provision for your family, and not being able to enter it at all. While on the face of it the present arrange-
ment seems eminently fair, and one can understand that the commanding officers in England naturally want to promote men who have been overseas for some considerable time; while one can understand the reasonableness of that attitude and their desire to promote men with whom they are familiar, I question whether it is in the interest of efficiency of the service. Certainly the result is that we have throughout our whole training set-up in the Dominion of Canada too many A category men who cannot be forced to revert, who cannot afford to revert, and who are stuck in this country by virtue of that regulation, when they would prefer to be on the other side of the ocean. If there is any disposition to doubt that, I will give you a list of a hundred odd of them. I know whereof I speak.
With respect to the question of discharges from the service, there has been some improvement since I spoke to the committee before. With respect to discharging men from the present army discretion has rested in the district officers commanding to take men who are in C category and who have jobs to go to, and discharge them from the service and return them to civilian life. To the best of my knowledge that authority has not been abused. On the other hand, under this present system of reviewing these men by the personnel selection boards, we have a certain number coming back from basic and even from advanced training centres of a category which makes it unlikely that they will become efficient soldiers. They are sent back for duty in a depot, for example, where duties do not exist in any considerable numbers, and we are having a considerable number of these men being boarded out on medical grounds. In effect it means that they are classed mentally deficient; that is to say they are incapable of assimilating military training in the prescribed time.
We have not in this country anything in our army in the nature of a labour battalion. I know the arguments against the labour battalion, and I am not particularly hopeful of a sympathetic hearing for what I wish to say with respect to that. I do say, nevertheless, that there is a place in every district for, perhaps, a labour company. There are duties to be performed, particularly in winterized camps, permanent camps, which could be performed by men of this category, who would be more usefully employed in this war effort than they would be by being returned to civilian life. That is debatable, no doubt, but in my experience and in my opinion it is unquestionably true. I am not looking for labour battalions in the sense of a refuge for crocks, as has happened at times in the past.

War Appropriation
But useful men can and should be employed. When I have made that suggestion on occasion I have been told, "Oh, there is a farm labour shortage; let those men who are unable to take training go back and work on the farms." Well, this country has paid the price of the thought, conceived mostly by city people, that anyone can farm. If men are not able to assimilate basic training at the present time, it is very doubtful whether they would be of any use in the war-speeded industry in the Dominion of Canada, and I am quite sure that they would be largely useless under the pressure of modern agriculture. So if anything can be made of their training and their physical condition-and I think it can-we should have organized in every district labour companies for the purpose of performing these duties.
It has been said frequently, and the minister has suggested again to-day, that it is impossible to have any real elasticity or any individual responsibility in an army, and I suggest to the minister that, while channels for the evolution and development of new ideas exist, they get horribly clogged at times. I am not going to use either the expression "bottleneck", or to try to suggest where it is. But I do know this, that it takes a long time for ideas to reach the place where they can be carried into effect; they are quite often not recognizable when they get there, and if they are good, sometimes they have even changed their paternity. But there is provision for that within the army itself. Not only the junior officers but the men in the ranks are being encouraged, if they have ideas, to report them and bring them forward. Some hon. members know the routine. It goes from the private to the sergeant, from the sergeant to the sergeant-major, from the sergeant-major to the company commander, from the company commander to the adjutant, from the adjutant to the colonel; and I do not pretend to follow it after it reaches district headquarters-it is supposed to go to national defence headquarters; but if everybody does his duty and anyone who is responsible sees it within three months, it is a miracle. Somewhere in the senior ranks of national defence headquarters there should be somebody to whom any private can write a letter and give his ideas. It does not matter how goofy it is, it won't be any crazier than some you get at times from the higher ranks, and if you get only one that is of real value, that officer's time will have been well spent.
Regarding our training, in connection with the general set-up, we are told in one breath that every soldier, under conditions of modern warfare, is his own general. I have been told
that by training officers who have had experience on the other side in this war. I have listened to it with approval, and I hope that in fact it is being carried out.' But we are told almost in the same breath that if the officer commanding a district in British Columbia wants an extension on his telephone, he will probably have to get treasury board approval for it. Somewhere between those extremes the truth may lie. I have no doubt the minister is working on it.

The question of forming a labour battalion has been mentioned. There is one suggestion which I would offer the minister, and I shall be glad to hear his reply, to see whether it is within the realms of possibility. In southern Alberta there are a large number of people who have very strong convictions against handling rifles or shedding blood. It would seem that the young men in these particular groups or colonies would want to take part in this great struggle, and would want to hold their heads up with other young men and be regarded as Canadians. In 1923 a colony came in to one particular municipality and since that time they have doubled their holdings, and six new groups have come into the same municipality. They find that by their way of living and through their farming practices they are able to extend rapidly. The provincial government have recognized the danger and have passed a law to prevent these people from acquiring more land for the duration of the war. The population is about 1,866, and 700 of them belong to the Hutterite colony. Ordinary people of that municipality feel quite keenly on this point. They consider that in this great democracy all should be on the same basis and that these particular people should be on the same basis as other Canadians. Everyone realizes that they are protected by an agreement, order in council P.C. 1678

passed on August 12, 1899. At that time no one anticipated that we would be in the condition we are now in, such great changes have taken place. Inasmuch as there are a large number of these people, my suggestion is that the agreement might be reviewed to see whether all parties have lived up to it, and whether some of these young men could be enrolled in a labour battalion to do certain work. I have consistently hesitated about taking on anything more in connection with the Department of National Defence than matters relating strictly to the military effort. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) the other day advocated the same idea with regard to a group of citizens out west as we have heard this afternoon from the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch). The question of labour battalions is in mind. We have employment platoons whom we have been using in camps and in connection with special work in the way of fatigues and things of that sort. If labour battalions are necessary in connection with army activities, that is one thing, and I am willing to consider it. If, however, you are only forming a labour battalion, or using the Department of National Defence to form a labour battalion, for the purpose of doing civilian work on parks or other projects of that sort, then I suggest that it should not be under this department. The hon. member for Lake Centre had the better idea, that is, to allow the Department of National War Services to call them up, if that is necessary, and form a battalion, if you like to call it that; but it should be under some department other than National Defence. We have a good many activities and we are trying to keep our eyes on the target, which is to fight the enemy, and not to deal with matters which are extraneous, even though in connection with them organization might be useful. I will take into consideration the question as it affects army activities, but that is as far as I should like to go in that respect.
With regard to the matters mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg South, I spent a very fruitful and profitable three hours with the adjutant-general and Brigadier Chisholm, who is in charge of personnel selection, last Sunday on this very point to which my hon. friend has referred. He is right with regard to the matter of examinations. I think that the number of discharges could have been reduced substantially had the discharge taken place at the other end, in the sense that they

War Appropriation
should never have been accepted. The test for mental aptitude has not been sufficient;
I am satisfied about that. As hon. members know, the test has been made entirely by medical boards. There is a very general provision in the medical regulations with regard to aptitude, and I am sure that a certain number of doctors have felt themselves not qualified to pass on that phase of a man's ability to serve. They have found him A, so far as physical condition was concerned, and have let it go at that; but very often the man has not been able to keep up training, so that you find him in the group, of whom many are going to North Bay for what the air force would call a cease training course. The air force had the same idea in connection with their work, and it has been, by the way, under a member of this house, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey). We are doing the same thing, and I do agree that a change is called for, and it has been made. '
As I explained the other night, the directorate of personnel selection has not been functioning for more than six months, and weeding out has taken place as a result of the activities of that branch. To some extent the medical regulations are now being amended and provision is being made with regard to a test, I will not call it a psychological test, but rather an aptitude test, which is being given. Provision is being made for supplying medical boards with additional skilled help if needed to deal with aptitude as well as with physical condition. As the hon. member hinted, the men available for that are not too plentiful across Canada, and we have' provided for special instruction for groups of men. They will not be fully trained in that respect, but will understand the fundamentals which are needed to find out whether a man gives good promise of becoming an efficient soldier. Hon. members know that there is a small discharge from the air force, and the disparity in that regard has struck me as one calling for an exhaustive investigation. The short way of explaining it is this. The air force requires, so far as educational qualifications are concerned, that men shall have gone to the eighth grade, whereas the army qualification is practically one of literacy. Practically, that is all that is required, if the man is to take the training laid down; and perhaps the severest feature in the matter of literacy is the map reading under the basic training syllabus. He is then taken on, and the men who are not up to that standard are finding it difficult to get along. That is why the change is being made and a new organization is being set up.

This afternoon the hon. member for York West raised a question which has given me some considerable difficulty. It is the case of a young chap who enlists, and who applies for a dependents' allowance for his mother. Quite frequently the board will point out that at the time the young chap enlisted, his family were on direct relief; that he was not making any cash contribution to the upkeep of the household, and in such cases the allowance is. not granted. It seems to me that these matters should be considered on the basis of necessity. If the family required assistance, and the young chap was not able to obtain gainful employment, I believe the allowance should be granted. I know of many applications that have been refused on the ground I have mentioned.
I am sorry I was not in the house last Tuesday, but I read in Hansard the discussion which took place between the hon. member for Lethbridge and the minister as to responsibility for the hospitalization of soldiers' dependents. The way I dealt with it was to indicate that the dependents' board of trustees, which was established in November or December, has as one of its functions and one of its authorities to pay such supplementary grants or to give such special assistance in those cases where it is satisfied that such supplementary grants or special assistance are necessary to prevent hardships arising because of unusual circumstances. . . .

Does my hon. friend wish me to answer that now? I understand that he is speaking about the hospitalization of dependents. What I said was that there was some suggestion from hon. members that this was the responsibility of the municipality. That is fundamentally so. I said that under the provisions of the dependents' board of trustees-I have not the exact terms before me at the moment-there is a regulation which permits the board to pay grants or give assistance in emergent cases or cases of hardship, such as the serious illness of members of the family. It is extending the Pension Act and the provisions of the dependents' allowance board beyond what I should think they were ever intended to cover if one were to say that when a soldier enlists he is entitled to his pay and allowances, his wife is entitled to separation allowance, his dependents are entitled to allowances, and the family are entitled to hospitalization. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Perhaps I may deal with some of the questions asked by my hon. friend. I think his first question was as to the number of men called up to the basic training centres. The total number called for four months training up to April 9, 1942, was 41,606, with an additional 10,730 who already had received thirty days of training and who were called up for the remainder of

War Appropriation
their training. That makes a total of 52,336. My hon. friend asked then how many came out. I am sorry I have not those figures here, but the hon. member will realize that we cannot get the reports concerning those who were called up in January for another month or two, because the first class of those who entered the camps in January will not be coming out until May, and so one cannot tell how many of those called up since January will graduate or come out of the training centres.
Then the hon. member asked as to the proportion of enlistments. I gave a statement to the committee on this question the other day, giving the number of men called out under the national war services regulations who, while under training, have enlisted voluntarily in the armed services. Of the four months classes, beginning March 20, 1941, and ending with the class which went in on October 2 and graduated on January 31 [DOT]-I have not the enlistments from the training centres since that time, but the other night I indicated to the hon. member for Lake Centre that I thought those enlistments during that time would be in the neighbourhood of between three and four thousand.
The number who actually were accepted in that period between March 20, 1941, and October 2, 1941, was 25,892. That is, they were accepted in training centres. The number enlisting in the Royal Canadian Navy was 322; in the army, 6,185, and in the air force, 2,843, making a total of 9,350; or 36 per cent of all of those who were accepted in the training centres enlisted in one of the three services. I believe that percentage has been pretty well kept up. I cannot tell my hon. friend for certain, but I believe I used the same percentage when I estimated between
3,000	and 4,000 for January, February and March.
My hon. friend asked if there were battalions which have in them home defence personnel and active service personnel. Most of the battalions in the sixth and seventh divisions at the present time, and most of the artillery units as well, have both home defence personnel and general service personnel-and I prefer to use that expression-in the same units. My hon. friend has asked whether I favour that method. My reply is there are things to be said for it and things to be said against it. But from the practical point of view it was impossible to have these home defence personnel as they came out of training centres go to a separate unit. In order to give them training and get them used to operational work both in the artillery and as coast defence battalions it was necessary to have them gradually come into the units. We
figured it was on a basis of about 10 per cent a month, so that they would be gradually absorbed in battalions or batteries, as the case may be. At the same time that releases general service personnel which could go overseas and follow the inclinations for which they originally enlisted.
With regard to the home defence personnel I would say that when I was out west there was some complaint about it. I can quite understand that complaint, because I had the same complaint when I was overseas in the last war. Men came to us who had come in under the Military Service Act of the last war. But those men came in and were absorbed in the battalions.
People are saying we should use the manpower of this countxy. We cannot use the man-power of this country, I submit, if we are not willing to take these men in and train them for operations. When I was talking to officers there I said, "You are commanding officers, and are training battalions for operation; you are citizens of Canada as well. You want to see the man-power of Canada utilized, and the way to utilize those men to the best advantage is to have them come to units and gradually become acclimated so that they may be able to carry on."
That is the situation with regard to this personnel and, as my hon. friend knows, I regard the units as active units. Certain of the personnel cannot be sent out of Canada except, as the Prime Minister explained, under the War Measures Act; and certain of them can. When the time came either the War Measures Act could be used, or other personnel could be put into the units, or these men could volunteer. Those are the three alternatives.
My hon. friend has asked if dependents' allowances were the same for home defence and general service personnel, and the answer is yes. He has asked whether payments start from the time men are called up, or after they have completed training. The answer is that dependents' allowances start at the same time as the pay.
I know the hon. member has asked a number of questions I have not answered; but I am endeavouring to answer the questions immediately, rather than leave them over. If he would remind me of others I would be pleased to give answers.
