speechtext: For several days we have been considering that portion of the war appropriation bill which provides funds for the army for the fiscal year beginning on April 1 of this year and ending on March 31 of next year. Hon. members who are interested will find the break-down of the army's portion of the war appropriation at page 1688 of Hansard. The total amount for the army is $997,000,000-in other words, practically half of the total amount provided in the war appropriation bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is for what?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
For the army. Breaking that expenditure down again we find that almost exactly half the money for the army is to provide funds for Canadian formations and functions at present overseas, including increments. The amount under that heading is approximately $495,000,000. Then, over a quarter of the balance of the money for the army is for Canadian formations and functions to be sent overseas during the fiscal year 1942-43, the amount being slightly over $135,000,000. The balance of the army's appropriation is to be spent on formations in Canada.
It seems to me the committee would be well advised at this stage to try to get a broad picture of Canadian army activities both abroad and at home. First of all, we have our Canadian army in Great Britain. It is an army of which the Canadian people may well be very proud and one which, I am sure, will live up to and perhaps surpass- although that will be difficult-the traditions of the Canadian corps in the last war. That army in Great Britain can be sent anywhere; there are no strings on where the men can serve.
We have another army in Canada which cannot be sent anywhere. The one exception, I believe, is the fourth division which is preparing to go overseas. As the minister has just

said, most of the units of this army contain home defence personnel, soldiers who have been called up under the National Eesources Mobilization Act which was passed by this house in June, 1940. As hon. members know, this act provides that men called up cannot be required to serve outside of Canada. The act is chapter 13 of the statutes of 1940, and section 2 gives the governor in council the power of-

requiring persons to place themselves, their services and their property at the disposal of His Majesty in the right of Canada, as may be deemed necessary or expedient for securing the public safety, the defence of Canada-
And so on, but there is another section, section 3, which contains a restriction and which reads:
The powers conferred by the next preceding section may not be exercised for the purpose of requiring persons to serve in the military, naval or air forces outside of Canada and the territorial waters thereof.
The minister has just told us that there are 15,269 men, known as home defence personnel, who were called up under the act and accordingly are subject to the restriction contained in section 3. They are scattered throughout the various units of the army in Canada. As we all know, there are many more of this same class of soldier training in the training centres. Some weeks ago either the Minister of National Defence or the Prime Minister said that the seventh and eighth divisions, which are to be raised this year for the defence of the east and west coasts, would be composed largely of men called up under the National Eesources Mobilization Act. This means that these divisions cannot be used beyond the boundaries of Canada or the territorial waters thereof. If this restriction were removed our army in Canada, like our army in Great Britain, could be used anywhere.
In my opinion, and I cannot emphasize this too strongly, that is necessary for the army on the Pacific coast. They will probably have to go abroad sooner or later, either to the adjoining state of Washington on the mainland, or to some of the islands which form part of that state, or to Alaska or Siberia. They may have to cross the ocean to fight. Let us always remember that Canada must avenge Hong Kong, and we cannot do that on this side of the Pacific ocean. Hong Kong must be avenged across the Pacific, and so far as Canada is concerned that can be done only by troops who go from the Canadian Pacific coast.
This Canadian army may have to serve in Australia. It may be that fighting in Australia will be the best way to defend the Pacific

War Appropriation
coast of Canada, just as fighting in Great Britain or on the continent of Europe is considered by the government to be the best way to defend our Atlantic coast. The Prime Minister pointed out the wisdom of such a course in his radio address on the plebiscite on April 7, when he used these words:
One thing is perfectly certain. If the enemy is not kept at bay on the oceans, and defeated beyond the waters of the Atlantic and the Pacific, the final battles of the world conflict will be fought in the waters and upon the soil of Canada and the United States.
I repeat that the Canadian army on the Pacific should be composed of men who can go anywhere. Then they could take their part in the attack on Japan which must eventually come. May I point out to the minister that Canada should be building, and building speedily, an "Army of the Pacific". This should be composed, not only of men who can be sent anywhere, but men who have been trained just as thoroughly as the troops in Great Britain. Men who have been completely trained should not be taken from this army, as has happened in recent months, to be replaced by men who are only partly trained. That sort of thing should stop. Once the men in this "Army of the Pacific" have been trained, they should be left there and not drawn away as drafts to be sent overseas or to some other part of Canada. This army should be equipped as completely as the Canadian army in Great Britain and it should be supported by an adequate air force and by units of the various types that are needed in modern warfare. This has not been done. There is nothing even remotely approaching a set-up of that kind provided for the "Army of the Pacific" in Canada.
In this war Canada has two fronts, the Atlantic front and the Pacific front. Let the Canadian government, this House of Commons and the Canadian people realize that clearly. If they do not, sooner or later disaster may strike this nation. On the Atlantic front Canada is preparing to fight an offensive war in or from Great Britain; on the Pacific front she is preparing to fight, not an offensive but a defensive war. She is preparing merely to hold on, to fight a holding war. The Prime Minister in his radio speech, from which I quoted a few minutes ago, summed up the effect of such a policy quite clearly with these words:
We cannot defend our country and save our homes and families by waiting at home for the enemy to attack us. Every country that has stood behind its own defences in this war has
sooner or later been attacked. To remain on the defensive is the surest way to bring the war to Canada.
Yet that is exactly the policy that is being followed by this got ernment so far as the "Army of the Pacific ' is concerned. On the other hand, the United States is fighting an offensive war on the Pacific. Troops are being sent abroad to various centres where they may meet the enemy far from American soil. If Canada pursues her present policy, and if the Japanese should attempt an invasion of this continent, the result may be that Canada's portion of the Pacific coast will be chosen for the attack. I point out these facts to the minister and to the hon. members because they merit the most careful consideration.
Let me ask hon. members to look again at the broad picture. What is parliament going to do about this situation of having units made up of men some of whom can be sent out of Canada and some of whom cannot?-a situation where one man in a company can say, "I do not have to go outside of Canada," while the man beside him has to go. That is, from a military point of view, and I am quite sure the minister will agree with me, placing a great handicap on our commanding officers and also on the troops themselves. What is parliament going to do about that situation? What is this House of Commons going to do about it? What are the members of this house going to do about it?
This week, only five days ago, the Canadian' people freed our hands. That can be clearly seen in an advertisement which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of April 25 asking for a "yes" vote. At the bottom of the advertisement we find these words, "Free Canada for all-out war. Vote yes." Now the Canadian people have spoken and our course is perfectly clear. It is, I suggest, to free our own hands at once; and free them without further delay, because if we do not act soon it will be impossible to amend the National Resources Mobilization Act before the fall. Action should be taken now, without further delay, to remove the restriction which we ourselves imposed in section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act. If we take that action we shall show the Canadian people-and the Canadian people are watching us very closely at this time and are much concerned over the sort of leadership the Canadian House of Commons is going to give-we shall show the Canadian people that this House of Commons means business, that the plebiscite was not just a sham and that we intend to keep faith with them.

War Appropriation

I say further that our course is clear also in this, that we must do more leading and less following behind, less running along behind our people in the grim business of waging relentless war. The Canadian people have been ahead of parliament and ahead of the government on most occasions from the very beginning of the war. That should be stopped now. We have in this House of Commons a grand opportunity to lead them, and I hope that the Canadian members of parliament will seize that opportunity and give courageous leadership, not only at this time and under these special circumstances, but also throughout the remainder of this grave but challenging period.

speechtext: I know the minister does not want to misquote me. Perhaps he did not follow me closely. What I said was this: I was advocating the building up an "Army of the Pacific" which could be used abroad, perhaps not as big as our army in Great Britain but an army that would be able to fight on its own, fight by itself. I said that we had not in British Columbia anything even remotely approaching such an army at the present time, and principally because the units are composed of men who cannot be sent beyond the boundaries of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Then my hon. friend was making two points. One point was that he was asking for the defence of the Pacific coast, and he was saying that there were two fronts in Canada. I know that he does recognize that, but sometimes when he has spoken I have wondered whether he did so, because he has been very strong in connection with the Pacific coast but seldom mentions the Atlantic.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I do not like to have a statement like that made, because on every occasion when I have spoken in this house with regard to the defence of Canada, while I have pressed the needs of the Pacific coast

naturally as I represent a Pacific coast riding-just as firmly and as definitely as I could I have always referred to the needs of the east coast as well. If the members from the minister's own province have not gumption enough to get up and urge that steps be taken to improve

the defence of the Atlantic coast, I do not think it helps very much to accuse somebody else who speaks of the needs of the Pacific coast of being unfair to Canada. The onus is just the other way. I say, give the Atlantic coast everything they need, and I have pleaded for that, not as strongly perhaps as I might have for the needs of the Pacific coast because I do not know all the facts. I do not appreciate the minister or any member getting up here and making accusations against me in that way. What he should be doing is speaking to the members of his own party who come from Nova Scotia, for example, and asking them why they do not get up and press the needs of the Atlantic coast. They are the people who should know them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend is simply setting up a straw man to knock him down again. I made no accusation against him. I said, and the members of the committee will bear me out, that there have been times in this house when my hon. friend has not seemed to realize that there were two fronts, but only one.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I object to that. The minister should withdraw that because his statement is incorrect. If he can quote anything from Hansard to show that I have ever taken that stand I am prepared to let it go. But if not, I ask him to withdraw it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is twenty minutes to six o'clock, and while I hope my hon. friend will refresh his memory by looking up Hansard, I will withdraw my statement and say nothing more about it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The minister is the one who should look up Hansard.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend was suggesting two things. He suggested an army of the Pacific and said that there was nothing like that now, and the reason there is nothing like that now, he says, is that there is no power to send men beyond the boundaries of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is one reason.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is there any other reason that my hon. friend suggests why there is not an army of the Pacific, in practice if not in name?.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Perhaps the minister would have been better off if he had been listening a little more closely as I spoke. I suggested that he should build up an "Army of the Pacific" with the idea that it would be able to strike out. I suggested that if should consist not only of men who could be sent anywhere but also of trained men, men who

War Appropriation
had received as thorough a training as our Canadian army in Britain. I said further that the practice should be stopped, if it is not already stopped, of taking away from the Pacific men who have been trained. Certainly within the last few months trained men have been taken away from there and sent elsewhere. I further suggested that such army should be equipped just as completely as our army in Great Britain, and that it should be adequately supported by the air force and the other arms of the service. The minister knows that it is not built up on that basis at all at the present time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I still think that my hon. friend's fundamental objection to the measures we are taking on the Pacific was the fact that the troops were not in a position to be ordered abroad. I can assure my hon. friend that in the other respects every attention is being given and every effort is being made to form an army of the Pacific, not in name but in effect. I do not know of anything which is going forward with greater acceleration and more energy and vigour than that very thing of providing additional troops on the Pacific coast, and additional establishments for them, and training the men as fast as they can be trained. I can also assure my hon. friend that we are equipping them to the fullest extent we can provide, having regard to all the necessities with respect to equipment in active theatres.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is that army being built up as a striking force which could be used to strike, say, in Alaska, if necessary, or in Siberia? Is it the intention of the department to build up an army of that type, or is the department merely building up an army to hold the coast?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The department is not going to state its intentions with regard to what it is going to do with the army. What it is doing is building up two divisions, the seventh and eighth, and my hon. friend knows as well as anybody else the way divisions are built up. You have to start with the divisions themselves and carry on training and equipment in the normal way. What these divisions will be used for afterwards or where they may best be disposed are matters which will have to be dealt with as the circumstances arise. A large proportion of those two divisions are being provided and established near or adjacent to the Pacific coast.
With regard to the other matter, his question is, what will happen as a result of the plebiscite? That is really what my hon. friend was after.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I meant exactly what I said. The minister need not say what I was trying to aim at. If he can understand English he knows what I said. There were no hidden motives or anything of that type. He need not try to drape them around me.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: He answered my hon. friend.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend need not be short about it. The situation is that that is the effect of what my hon. friend was saying.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is the minister's interpretation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I can only say, with regard to sending men out of the country, the Prime Minister has already indicated that, as far as going to the Aleutian islands or to Washington is concerned, there would be no hestita-tion in using at any time the provisions of the War Measures Act for that purpose, if occasion arises. I do not think that that is what was in my hon. friend's mind. I think he had in mind an expeditionary force: although he speaks of an "Army of the Pacific", it is an expeditionary force he is thinking of.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. The minister is trying to put words in my mouth.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Then I will say, I suggest that that is what he has in mind.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I did not make any suggestion at all. I wish the minister would leave my speech as it is and not try to twist it around.	*

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I say, I suggest that what he has in mind is an expeditionary force. That matter will be dealt with and taken care of when the time comes. The situation at the present time is this. The hon. member speaks of trained men being taken away. Men are coming from these units and going overseas, and men who come from training centres are taking their place. That is the situation with regard to units on the Pacific coast now-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
If the hon. member will let me finish the sentence; I say, my hon. friend suggests that that is not the way it is done. I only say that in the last war battalion after battalion after battalion was broken up in Canada and used for reinforcements. What we are doing here is maintaining the battalion and sending trained men to take the place of the men who are going overseas. I have been through that experience in the last war. It is not a figment of the imagination.
War Appropriation

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The minister has missed the point.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have tried to make another one, anyway.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is what I object to. He is trying to make two or three other ones. The point I was trying to make was that there should be set up an army of the Pacific, just as we have an army in Great Britain. I think it is unwise, when you have sent men into British Columbia, for this "Army of the Pacific", and they have finally become trained, to take them away from their units and send them-I don't know where, but I know and the minister knows that that has been done in the last few weeks, and raw recruits sent in, when the position is such that there might be an attack on that coast at any time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: In the first place, the men who were taken away, if I understand the situation correctly, were men who were going overseas-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I don't know. They may have been taken east for instruction.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: -and the raw recruits, as my hon. friend calls them, were men from the training centres who had had four months' training. There may have been some raw recruits among them, I do not know, but generally they were men who came from the training centres. Surely my hon. friend does not mean to lay it down as a military proposition that you must maintain the same units in the same job all the time. If you have men who are fit for general service, who have enlisted for general service, and who want to go overseas, and you have men to take their places, there is no reason why you should not use the man-power of Canada for that purpose. It is still an "Army of the Pacific" to use my hon. friend's expression. They serve and they are trained; they are armed, and they are prepared to carry on-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: May I put it this way-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit me to finish the sentence? The only trouble in my hon. friend's mind is that they cannot be sent beyond the bounds of Canada. So far as the Aleutian islands and Washington are concerned the Prime Minister has indicated that he is prepared to send them any time it is necessary. With regard to sending them as an expeditionary force to Australia, or to Japan, that is another matter, which has to do more with the result of the plebiscite.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: With regard to this question of taking away trained men, consider this example. Suppose a regiment of artillery is sent into the Pacific area only partly trained; the training is completed and that unit is ready to fight, and then say half the regiment are taken away, sent I do not know where, and replaced by green men without that training. I submit to the minister that, in view of the danger of attack on the coast, that is not a very wise thing to do. That sums up my complaint-the taking away of men, once they are trained and prepared to fight, and replacing them by green men. The comparison with the last war is not a fair one, because at that time the fighting was all done in Europe. This time the fighting may be done in Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: All I will say to my hon. friend is, with regard to the illustration he gives, that taking away half the men at one time and replacing them with green men, certainly would not be wise. But I do not think that his hypothesis is correct, on either ground-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My proportion may be
wrong.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: -either that they were green men or that half were taken away. I believe the practice is to release not more than ten per cent of the strength at one time and substitute them with men from training centres.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
With
regard to this question which has arisen-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: With due respect to the leader of the opposition, I saw the hon. member for Temiscouata.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Well, I
have been on my feet three times.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I regret I must state that I rose two or three times before the hon. gentleman. The answer to part of the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South is to be found in Hansard of April 23, at page 1905. It is a quotation from a statement by Major-General Browne. Here is what the hon. member said:
I think General Browne gave the picture quite clearly when he was quoted as saying at that time, "The reserve force may have to fight and it must be ready to fight as soon as possible." he said. "After all, there is no more war overseas than there is here now, and we may have some here sooner than they have, in view of the threats to our coast."

War Appropriation
This is the declaration of an experienced soldier, and we find it on the lips of my hon. friend. It is to the effect that this country is threatened. The hon. member quoted a speech of our revered leader to the same effect, and all ministers have spoken the same way. The Minister of Justice said that Japan and Germany had their eyes on Canada, and even an admiral has stated that before long submarines were expected to come into the St. Lawrence river. I am not revealing any secret. All those statements can be found in public records, either in Hansard or in the press of the country. The question that we are discussing now is high above the heads of the Minister of National Defence, his colleagues and all of us. I am greatly sur-'rised that the present discussion is not being carried on in camera. I am all for complete information- to be given by ministers, but I find that information such as that which has been given this afternoon publicly by the minister-I do not complain about information being given, because I want to have information-is not such as should be given publicly. It has been stated by our Minister of National Defence this afternoon that the number of troops in our home guard in Canada is 15,000, if I heard rightly, and that is information which might be very valuable to the enemy. I am the last one to refuse information to the press if it is not as dangerous as this, if it is information that would not be used against us by the enemy.
I want to be clearly understood. Like the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), I want complete information; but I repeat, that information should be given in camera without any strangers in the gallery. It should be given for the benefit of hon. members who have a right to know what is the policy of the government. What I say now I do not say for the purpose of suggesting to the minister that he should refuse any information about the conduct of the war, about our home forces, about our forces overseas, or about munitions or anything like that. What I suggest is that there are things printed in the press that should not be so printed. I do not accuse members of the press gallery or owners of their newspapers. They take what is given to them, and they do well to take it when it is publicly given. But in view of the very difficult time through which we are passing it is important that we meet together, without any party consideration, to get all possible available information, and to keep it for ourselves, simply making any suggestions which we may see fit to offer to the Minister of National Defence.
Here is where I disagree with the hon. member for Vancouver South. He is all for the
defence of British Columbia, and in that regard I agree with him. I know that he is broadminded enough to concede that members from other parts of the country want those parts of the country defended as well as British Columbia.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I know that. But this is the point on which I do not agree with him. He suggested some time ago that some troops should be sent to Australia as a token of friendship. We have the greatest possible admiration for the wonderful people of Australia, but what is their trouble? Why did they call on the United States to send them men? It was because the Anzacs were in all parts of the world except in their own country. That is why they had to call on the United States for help; and as the hon. member for Vancouver South complains that the defence of his great province is not now what it should be, that is one more reason for not sending any human token to Australia in these times.
My second objection to what he said is this. He said that, in view of the answer which was given by the Canadian people in the plebiscite, section 3 of the Mobilization Act should be amended so as to send our men anywhere, wherever they are needed. I disagree with him completely. I would have no objection to conscription for service overseas if we had such a supply of men as to ensure our complete home defence first. Then we could send the overflow outside. But the answer "yes" to the plebiscite is not so much an answer "yes" to conscription overseas, as has been suggested by some hon. members. I say that for this reason. I have met English-speaking members of this house, for whom I have the greatest respect, as I have for all hon. members, and they have told me that they were positively opposed to conscription, and their electors also, and that they voted "yes" just because they were told that conscription would not be imposed if they voted "yes."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Who told
them that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I will mention one, Senator Gouin, who said that over the radio, and he was introduced by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton). He said, "If you vote 'yes' in the plebiscite, the plebiscite is to keep conscription away"-and it is reported on the last page of Le Canada. I do not agree with him on that, but this was said over the radio, and the senator was introduced by a member of this house who was strongly in favour of "yes." These things should b* known to the country.
War Appropriation

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The senator was introducing the member?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
No; the member was
introducing the senator over the radio, and that appears in the headlines in Le Canada. I have other quotations like that, and it is well known by all French members who read Le Canada. The suggestion I have made to the government is twofold: first, to improve our means of communication throughout this country, so as to facilitate the transport of troops from one point to another in case of emergency; and, second, to have mobile units. One hon. gentleman said that our army was more mobile than any other. That is true. No soldiers are left here; they have all gone away; it is a mobile army. My idea is that this country should be defended first. It must be defended precisely for the reasons given by our military leaders, the leaders of the army as well as of the navy, by the Prime Minister, and by all his colleagues. I find it most illogical to say that this country is threatened, when at the same time we have no men to defend it. It is more important to have men to defend the country, when the country is the arsenal of the empire; and this is one more reason why our enemies have had their eyes on this land.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Crerar the house adjourned at six p.m.
